text:
A: Hiya! Oh, you look exactly like your picture, the same smile!
B: [laughs] Hiya. Well, is the same face, yeah. I'm Agnieszka. Wolverhampton.
A: Sana, I'm in Bolton. Sorry, can you say your name again? I want to say it right.
B: Ag-nyesh-ka. Is okay, at school the kids call me Mrs A. Easier.
A: Agnieszka. Okay! Is that Polish?
B: Yeah, from Łódź. I'm here since 2006, so, long time now. I work in school office, primary school in Tettenhall. Attendance, dinner money, angry dads at front desk, you know?
A: Oh my God, angry dads. [laughs] Do you shout back?
B: No, no. I just say, okay, give it me, what is the problem, and usually is something small. A coat. Somebody lost a coat and is like end of the world.
A: [laughs] That's so funny. I do packing, in a warehouse, fashion stuff. My last call, the lady, she does care home, twelve hours, and I was complaining I'm tired from part-time. I felt so bad, honestly. She told me off for not finishing my course.
B: What course?
A: Lashes, beauty. I want to do my own business, mehndi and lashes, from home, Instagram. But I started it last year and, erm, it's sort of still sitting there.
B: Yeah, no, she's right. But also, you know, life. When I came here I had degree in economics and I was cleaning offices for two years. Six in the morning, hoovering. You don't always do the plan when you want.
A: Really? With a degree?
B: Yeah. My English wasn't good enough then, and nobody cares what is your degree from Poland. Then I did bookkeeping course at college here, then school job. So is fine. Slowly, slowly.
A: That's so good though. My English also was bad when I came, I did ESOL at Bolton College. The first years I was, honestly, so lonely, I didn't go anywhere except my mother-in-law's.
B: I understand that. Very much. Is your family here?
A: Only my husband's family. My mum and my sisters are in Lahore. I do voice notes with my sisters all day, all day. And video calls, and then after I cry. [laughs] Every time. My husband says why you call if you cry?
B: [laughs] Men. My mum is in Łódź, on her own now, seventy-eight. We do WhatsApp video every few days. And I think, should I bring her here? But she don't speak English, her friends are there, her church. Is difficult.
A: Yeah... that's hard. My mum would hate the weather here anyway. Lahore is so hot, and here it's like, rain, rain, rain.
B: [laughs] Same in Poland but colder. Winter in Łódź, minus fifteen. Here they close school for little bit of snow.
A: What do you do at the weekend then, if you're not at school?
B: Church on Sunday, Polish Mass. I walk with my neighbour every evening, Smestow Valley. And I grow tomatoes, this year very good tomatoes. Very proud.
A: Aww. I'm not sporty at all. I joined a gym, went five times, paid for months. [laughs] Don't tell anybody.
B: [laughs] Everybody did that once. Do you cook?
A: Every day, because Imran wants Pakistani food. Karahi, daal, roti. But I'm bored, I always say let's get Nando's. And at work I say tea now, not dinner, and barm. Barm cake. Do you say that?
B: No, here is bap! I buy baps for my daughter for lunch. When I came I didn't know any of these words. Bap, cob, barm, is all the same bread.
A: [laughs] English is so confusing, yaar.
